Would it be shocking to learn that Ole Miss officials had someone with FB...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich tells Lane Kiffin he should stand by his comments about Ole Miss, knowing he would hurt the school the whole time.

Would it be shocking to learn that Ole Miss officials had someone with FBI ties help check its football facility in the days following Lane Kiffin’s departure for LSU?

Sure, if college athletics were operating in anything resembling normal times.

But with former NFL players now finding paths back to college football and Congress debating legislation that could limit coaches from leaving during a season, almost nothing feels too absurd anymore.

NCAA Created This Mess, Now LSU Set To Make Dae’Quan Wright College Football’s First NFL Returnee

Walker Jones, the executive director of Ole Miss’ NIL collective, recently appeared on the "Assorted Crackers" podcast — yes, that is the name — to discuss the madness surrounding Kiffin’s exit for LSU.

Trinidad Chambliss of the Ole Miss Rebels celebrates on stage with teammates after the College Football Playoff quarterfinal game against the Georgia Bulldogs at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, La., on Jan. 1, 2026. (CFP/Getty Images)

During a conversation about coaches who were contractually tied to both Ole Miss and LSU, Jones revealed an unreported detail from the days leading up to the Rebels’ College Football Playoff appearance without Kiffin.

"We actually had the FBI come through and walk the building for bugs and for everything," Walker Jones told 'Assorted Crackers'". "We knew kind of what was in Baton Rouge, and we knew how they operated. I remember getting on my knees and looking underneath the desk, like checking for, 'Is there some sort of bug in my office?'"

PETE GOLDING DROPS UNFILTERED TRUTH ON 'EX' LANE KIFFIN, AND NCAA TAMPERING: 'WHAT HAVE WE CREATED?'

So, did Ole Miss bring in federal agents to sweep its facility for listening devices, straight out of a Jason Bourne movie?

Well, not exactly. But, yes there was a search.

On Monday, while Kiffin was fielding questions in Baton Rouge about LSU adding former NFL players to its roster, the questions in Oxford were a bit different.

What exactly happened with that FBI search of the Ole Miss football facility?

Head coach Pete Golding did not deny that a sweep occurred, though he offered an explanation that made far more sense than the image of agents descending on the Manning Center with bug detectors.

"Any bowl game, playoff system, obviously you're gonna up security," Golding told reporters. I'm not sure there was a hiring process of here we go with the FBI. I do think we probably have a current player whose dad just so happens to work for the FBI and that lives in town. There was no measure to go 'oh my gosh, come in from that standpoint'.

"Obviously any time you get into that playoff system and you got guys going from this building to other places (LSU), you want to make sure it's secure for your players. The video access, everything else you're doing regardless where you're at....No, there was no hiring process of 'let's get the FBI in here, holy cow, they start looking around'. It wasn’t anything like that."

Head coach Pete Golding of the Ole Miss Rebels looks on in the first half against the Miami Hurricanes during the College Football Playoff Semifinal at the VRBO Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Jan. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

When Kiffin left Ole Miss for LSU, he took multiple assistants with him to Baton Rouge. During the chaotic stretch before Ole Miss played Tulane in the College Football Playoff, some coaches were traveling back and forth between Baton Rouge and Oxford.

Kiffin was also expected to target multiple Ole Miss players once the Rebels’ season ended, including Kewan Lacy and Trinidad Chambliss.

LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES

Add in the growing paranoia across college athletics about practice footage and other team materials being illegally accessed through video databases, and it is not hard to understand why Ole Miss took extra precautions.

One of the most chaotic times in recent college athletics memory will one day turn into a movie that will have the feel of a spy-thriller directed by Michael Bay.

Just days before the season begins, coaches are explaining why former NFL players belong back on college rosters. The NCAA is spending what feels like every day in a courtroom. Congress is still being asked to fix a system that has become nearly impossible to govern.

And on Sept. 19, 2025, Ole Miss and LSU will meet in Oxford in a game that already feels destined to become one of the most entertaining weekends of the season.

Head coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers speaks during a press conference at the LSU Football Practice Facility in Baton Rouge, La., on Feb. 4, 2026. (Gus Stark/LSU/University Images)

PETE GOLDING MAKES IT KNOWN HE HAS TAMPERING RECEIPTS, WHILE ALSO ADMITTING KIFFIN TEXTS HIM WAY TOO MUCH

Between talk of "basket-weaving" classes at Ole Miss, Kiffin’s recruiting comments, eligibility lawsuits, Texas Tech’s Brendan Sorsby saga and endless congressional debates, college football needs actual games back in a hurry.

Still, who doesn’t enjoy a good FBI story in college athletics?

Well, perhaps Will Wade — or the folks at Michigan.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

articles.title: Beyond China's humanoid robots, a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
articles.excerpt:
Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workers

"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spend...
articles.body_text:
Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workers

"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

Students learning robotics at the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of many new vocational schools

It is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.

What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?

The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.

What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.

The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.

This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.

More than two millions robots work alongside people in China's factories

On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.

An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.

One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code.

"Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.

CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.

The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."

Pang Kai is part of the research and development team

A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.

The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages.

"In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.

Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.

The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?

"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."

Machines are part of every step in making Leapmotor's EVs

China has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand.

"China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics.

"If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."

However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.

Chinese innovation is powering the country's factories faster than expected

And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."

But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

China is winning one AI race, the US another - but either might pull ahead

Robot boxing, football and sprinting at World Humanoid Games

A decade on, Trump returns to a stronger and more assertive China

DeepSeek: How China's 'AI heroes' overcame US curbs to stun Silicon Valley

articles.title: Ambush in South Sudan kills peacekeeping troops
articles.excerpt:
An ambush has killed two United Nations peacekeepers in South Sudan.

The UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) said in a statement issued on Monday that armed men had ambushed a patrol as it travelled t...
articles.body_text:
An ambush has killed two United Nations peacekeepers in South Sudan.

The UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) said in a statement issued on Monday that armed men had ambushed a patrol as it travelled toward Pajut in Jonglei state. The attack comes as fears persist that the country risks sliding into a full-scale civil war.

The identities and nationalities of those killed have not yet been disclosed. Three other peacekeepers were wounded, along with two South Sudanese police officers and two civilian staff attached to the mission.

The UN peacekeeping mission said it deployed a “Quick Reaction Force” to secure the area and support the emergency response.

“Such deadly violence targeting UNMISS personnel, who are serving to support peace in South Sudan, is unacceptable,” Anita Kiki Gbeho, the head of the mission, said.

Numerous attacks on humanitarian workers have been recorded this year as the prospect of full-blown civil war rises, but violence against peacekeepers is rare.

UN figures show more than 450 attacks on humanitarian workers and assets between January and July, more than double last year’s total for the same period. At least 36 humanitarian workers and contractors were killed, surpassing the 31 killed across 2025.

The violence is playing out against months of grinding conflict between government troops and forces loyal to opposition leader Riek Machar.

Once vice president, Machar was suspended from the post last year and now sits under house arrest, facing treason charges he says are politically motivated.

His 2018 power-sharing agreement with President Salva Kiir has fallen apart, and South Sudan now finds itself edging toward a full civil war – a situation the deal was struck eight years ago to avoid.

Fighting escalated in December, when opposition forces seized government outposts in Jonglei. The government has hit back with air strikes and ground assaults, even as it insists it remains committed to the 2018 accord.

The United States, for its part, has kept pushing Kiir and Machar toward talks, calling earlier this year for “urgent action to uphold peace and mitigate the risk of civil war through an immediate return to dialogue among the parties to the 2018 peace agreement.”

articles.title: Mariska Hargitay nearly left 'Law & Order SVU' over fear of being a 'one-trick pony'
articles.excerpt:
Dennis Quaid spoke out about receiving the 2026 Patriot Ally Award at the 2nd Annual Military & Veteran Entertainment Awards Gala.

Mariska Hargitay once considered leaving "Law & Order: Special Victi...
articles.body_text:
Dennis Quaid spoke out about receiving the 2026 Patriot Ally Award at the 2nd Annual Military & Veteran Entertainment Awards Gala.

Mariska Hargitay once considered leaving "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" after more than two decades as Olivia Benson because she worried the role had come to define her career.

In a new interview with Variety, the actress — who has starred as Benson since "SVU" premiered in 1999 —  said she began questioning her future on the long-running NBC drama around its 25th season.

"I’ve got to leave the show too. I don’t want people to think I’m a one-trick pony," Hargitay recalled telling fellow "ER" co-star Julianna Margulies.

'THE BIG BANG THEORY' STAR JIM PARSONS SAYS HE PAID A STEEP PRICE FOR FAME

Mariska Hargitay explained why she nearly quit "Law & Order: SVU" during a new interview with Variety. (Getty Images; Michael Schwartz for Variety)

Margulies, who famously left "ER" after six seasons, had a blunt response.

"Sweetheart, that ship’s sailed," Hargitay said Margulies told her.

While Benson made her a household name, the Emmy winner admitted she often felt constrained creatively due to the grueling production schedule.

"The comedy thing was painful to me because I felt like I was only exercising one part of myself," Hargitay said. "People would say, ‘You need to get off that show and do comedy. You need to get off that show and have a talk show.’"

‘X-FILES’ STAR GILLIAN ANDERSON REVEALS PARENTING REGRET, SAYS SHE WISHES SHE WAS 'LESS SELFISH'

Hargitay has portrayed Olivia Benson since 1999.  (Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

"I wasn’t ready to leave, because I loved it," she said. "And then I got to do all this other stuff, and that’s why I don’t think about leaving right now. Do I want to quit now? No. Why? I made a movie while shooting; I did a play for six weeks on hiatus. I’m hosting the Emmys."

In 2023, Hargitay opened up to Fox News Digital about franchise creator and producer Dick Wolf's "great writing."

"Dick Wolf is truly a visionary," she said Tuesday. "And I think that's a very singular thing to be a true visionary who understands our culture in a very deep way, but also understands it's sort of ironic that a crime show would be actually calming in a way to our nervous system, knowing that somebody is out there taking care of it."

Mariska Hargitay said she's not thinking about leaving "SVU" anytime soon.  (Michael Schwartz for Variety)

She continued, "That our voices are heard and there are people that are on it. So that is it."

MARISKA HARGITAY JOKES ABOUT BEING LONGTIME ‘LAW & ORDER’ CO-STAR CHRIS MELONI'S ‘SECOND WIFE’

"It's a very sort of interesting dichotomy," Hargitay added. "Because you think about a crime show, which normally should sort of upset your nervous system, actually can settle it down because of that."

"Law & Order's" success spawned seven spinoffs including "Special Victims Unit," "Criminal Intent," "Trial by Jury," "LA," "UK," "True Crime" and "Organized Crime."

KELSEY GRAMMER ADMITS SURPRISING REASON 'FRASIER' ALMOST NEVER HAPPENED

The actress is gearing up to host the Emmys next month.  (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images)

In 2019, "SVU" became the longest-running live-action television series in history. Hargitay has starred as Detective Olivia Benson in the police procedural since its premiere in 1999 and became an executive producer in 2016.

Fox News Digital's Larry Fink contributed to this post.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: Oklahoma-based Southwest Airlines flight attendant found dead in Hawaii, police investigating
articles.excerpt:
Internet searches from conman Brian Walshe and voicemails from his mother, Diana, take center stage in new Fox Nation special on the Ana Walshe murder case.

An Oklahoma-based Southwest Airlines fligh...
articles.body_text:
Internet searches from conman Brian Walshe and voicemails from his mother, Diana, take center stage in new Fox Nation special on the Ana Walshe murder case.

An Oklahoma-based Southwest Airlines flight attendant was found dead outside her hotel in Hawaii.

A spokesperson for the Honolulu Police Department told Fox News Digital that an unattended death investigation was launched for 50-year-old Jenny Lupton, whose family says fell off the 24th floor of her hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii.

According to News9, Lupton's family was told by the Honolulu Department of the Medical Examiner that she fell from her balcony off the 24th floor, as she was staying at the Hilton Hawaiian Village in Waikiki.

AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANT KILLED IN TOURIST HOT SPOT AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE SUSPECTED BOAT STRIKE

Jenny Lupton, a Southwest Airlines flight attendant from Moore, Oklahoma, was found dead during a layover in Waikiki. She spent 29 years with the airline. (Jenny Lupton/Facebook)

Tresa Lupton, Jenny's sister, said the flight attendant went out with her co-workers.

CARNIVAL CRUISE SHIP PASSENGER DIES AFTER FALLING FROM BALCONY – FBI INVESTIGATES HIGH-SEAS HORROR

"She just went out with one of her flight attendant friends, and they danced and had a good time," said Tresa Lupton. "She had gotten a tattoo while she was there."

Jenny Lupton, 50, adored her 15-year-old son and was remembered by family as full of life. (Jenny Lupton/Facebook)

Tresa Lupton said her sister was in Hawaii due to work and planned to stay for a few days before returning to Oklahoma.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

According to Lupton's family, hotel security told them that police are reviewing over 70 cameras that were in the area. Police aren't sure if anyone witnessed the fall.

A Southwest Airlines 737 comes in for landing at Portland International Airport on Feb. 9, 2026. (iStock)

Tresa Lupton said she's traveling to Hawaii to search for her sister, saying "the timeline doesn’t make sense, and we are afraid that maybe there was foul play."

The Honolulu Police Department said it won't be releasing more information until its investigation is complete.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Southwest Airlines and Hilton Hawaiian Village in Waikiki.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: Manhunt for Massachusetts woman ends with grim discovery week after police officer husband found dead at home
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The body of a woman believed to be Karen Solomon, the missing wife of a veteran Worcester, Massachusetts, police offic...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The body of a woman believed to be Karen Solomon, the missing wife of a veteran Worcester, Massachusetts, police officer found dead last week, was discovered in city woods Monday with a handgun nearby, authorities said.

Worcester police said two employees at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding a deceased person in the woods near the facility at approximately 12:40 p.m.

"Upon further examination, we believe this person to be Karen Solomon," police said during a Monday news conference at Worcester police headquarters, stressing that the identification remains preliminary.

Investigators also recovered a handgun near the body, authorities said.

SPECIAL FORCES VET ACCUSED OF TRYING TO KILL WIFE FOUND DEAD, ENDING MASSIVE TENNESSEE MANHUNT

Karen Solomon, 58, was wanted by police in Massachsuetts. (Worcester Police Department)

The discovery came nearly a week after Solomon, 58, vanished following the death of her husband, Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon.

Police had been searching the Coes Pond area near Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital and had previously searched the same area on Aug. 20.

Karen Solomon had been sought since Kurt Solomon was found dead inside a Wildwood Avenue residence on Aug. 18.

Police responded to the residence at about 5:28 a.m. after receiving a report of a person down and found the off-duty Worcester police officer dead inside, authorities said. His cause and manner of death have not been released.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECT CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED POLICE OFFICER AND HIS GIRLFRIEND

Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. arrives at Westside Animal Clinic while law enforcement searches the Coes Pond area during the investigation involving Karen Solomon and the death of Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Authorities initially said Karen Solomon was a suspect they wanted to question about what happened inside the home.

Worcester police later released surveillance video and photographs of her as the search stretched into multiple days, warning the public that she was believed to be armed and dangerous.

The department said Solomon was last seen in pajama shorts and a tank top walking toward Westcott Street. A police spokesperson told Fox News Digital last week that she was still believed to be armed and the case remained a "very active investigation."

SUSPECTS IN DEADLY CONNECTICUT HOME INVASION ARRESTED IN ATTACK THAT ROCKED BEACH TOWN

Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon, a 31-year department veteran who was identified by the New England Police Benevolent Association after an off-duty officer was found dead at a Worcester home. (The New England PBA, Inc.)

Police have disclosed few details about what happened inside the residence, citing the ongoing investigation and domestic violence-related restrictions.

Public records reviewed by The Associated Press show Kurt and Karen Solomon co-owned the Wildwood Avenue residence. Kurt Solomon also identified Karen Solomon as his wife in a 2016 bankruptcy filing, according to the AP.

The New England Police Benevolent Association identified Kurt Solomon as a 31-year veteran of the Worcester Police Department and remembered him as an "incredibly dependable officer, colleague and friend."

"Thirty-one years of service represents an extraordinary commitment to a community and to the profession of law enforcement," the association said. "Officer Kurt Solomon answered that call for more than three decades, and his service, friendship and dedication will not be forgotten."

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Trump inauguration pastor says Dearborn Christians 'afraid' to speak out in Muslim-majority city
articles.excerpt:
Pastor Lorenzo Sewell accuses city officials of giving Muslims ‘preferential treatment’ and allowing a ‘two-tiered justice system.’

A Detroit pastor who delivered a prayer at President Donald Trump’s...
articles.body_text:
Pastor Lorenzo Sewell accuses city officials of giving Muslims ‘preferential treatment’ and allowing a ‘two-tiered justice system.’

A Detroit pastor who delivered a prayer at President Donald Trump’s inauguration says Christians in Muslim-majority Dearborn, Michigan, have privately told him they are afraid to publicly express their faith, while accusing local officials of giving Muslim residents preferential treatment under a "two-tiered justice system."

"Right now, the city officials in Dearborn specifically, they are giving Muslims preferential treatment," Lorenzo Sewell, senior pastor of 180 Church in Detroit, told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday.

"Now, how do I know that?" Sewell asked. "This is how I know that. Being a Black man in the city of Detroit, we go to Dearborn. We know that the police know how to enact justice in Dearborn. They know how to pull you over. They know that if they catch you shoplifting, we've had Black women that tried to elude the police and lost their lives in the city of Dearborn."

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

President Donald Trump and Rev. Lorenzo Sewell of 180 Church in Detroit at Trump's inauguration in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol on January 20, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Ricky Carioti - Pool/Getty Images)

"So, as a Black man that has grown up around Arabs my entire life, I know that the Dearborn police can enact justice," he continued. "So, when someone is being assaulted and nothing happens, when someone's being assaulted and the police choose to look the other way, you can see clearly a two-tiered justice system."

"So, the city council, instead of them renouncing Sharia law, they are actually upholding Sharia law," Sewell added.

Sewell recently went viral following remarks he gave at a Dearborn town hall where he said, "America, we have lost this city. This is a city that is no longer up under American laws; we are up under Sharia law. We will not have it anymore."

FORT WORTH PRINCIPAL PICK FACES BACKLASH, INVESTIGATION OVER SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS DEFENDING SHARIA LAW

Dearborn Mayor Abdullah H. Hammoud told CBS News that there are nearly 30 Christian churches in Dearborn and more than a dozen mosques. (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)

CBS News reported last Wednesday that Dearborn police said they made 22 arrests following the "Christian Crusader March," led by conservative activist Jake Lang. Sewell attended the march, which took place near a regularly scheduled Dearborn City Council meeting where he later delivered his viral remarks.

In a statement, Dearborn Police Chief Issa Shahin said, "Our officers met a challenging and rapidly evolving situation with the professionalism this community expects, keeping everyone safe, protecting the constitutional rights of those who came to be heard, and allowing the City Council to complete its business. I could not be prouder of them."

DOJ WEIGHS CIVIL RIGHTS PROBE INTO FORT WORTH POLICE OVER ALLEGED FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATIONS

Sewell told Fox News Digital he is concerned about the growing presence of what he called Sharia law practices in the community.

"One of the examples that I see of Sharia law happening right here in the metro Detroit … in the city of Hamtramck, you are allowed right now to sacrifice animals, literally," Sewell said. "Number two, halal meat. If you go to a public school, you are literally eating meat that's sacrificed to idols, because, according to Sharia law, that's what — that's a lawful meat."

Lorenzo Sewell, the pastor of 180 Church, speaks at a Dearborn City Council meeting on Aug. 8, 2026. (Dearborn City)

"And I believe the most concerning to me is the call to prayer," he added. "There is no other place in the world that you can go and tell that country, although you are a majority Christian country, you can't go anywhere else in the nation and tell that country they have to change the way they express their religious beliefs."

CALIFORNIA LAWMAKERS' PUSH TO MAKE MUSLIM HOLY DAYS STATE HOLIDAYS SPARKS DEBATE OVER SCHOOL NEUTRALITY

In January 2023, the Hamtramck City Council voted to allow animal sacrifice, and the website for Dearborn Public Schools says, "Dearborn Public Schools ensures all meats served in our schools are certified Halal."

The certificate for the halal meat, partially in Arabic, reads in part, "We certify that the food processing facility of Saad Wholesale, Inc. in Detroit, MI, USA has been inspected and approved by our Islamic organization for processing, packing, and labeling of Halal Meat & Poultry Products by applying our procedures according to the Islamic Rites."

"I see the city council upholding Sharia law through things like the call to prayer, through things like halal meat, through having more Arab writing than they do actually English, by having the chief of police talk more about protecting the rules of Islam and Islamic leaders instead of protecting the rights of all Americans," Sewell continued.

Detroit Pastor Lorenzo Sewell told Fox News Digital that Christians in Muslim-majority Dearborn, Michigan, have privately told him they are afraid to express their faith. (iStock)

"So you can see clearly when someone speaks freely, they can be attacked, and it'd be justified," he added. "I can give you a clear example. My wife had her life threatened. We had the guy's number, we had his address, we had everything, and the lieutenant did absolutely nothing. So, that's how you can see a two-tier justice system."

DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH

He also claimed that Christians in the area feel afraid to express their faith.

"Since I went viral, I've had Dearborn Christians come out from the north, south, east, and west, and they're afraid," Sewell said. "I want you to think about this for a moment, America. Think about being in a Christian nation, being afraid to talk about Christ. I want you to just think about that for a moment."

"I'm having people say, 'I'm with you, but I'm afraid to say it,'" he continued. "'I'm with you, but I'm afraid to be by you.' 'I'm with you —' This is how we know we are in a two-tiered system because, in a Christian nation, we're afraid to be Christians."

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

Dearborn, Michigan resident Andrea Unger started a petition in 2025 to pressure the city council to enforce a noise ordinance after two years of a local mosque broadcasting its calls to prayer over a loudspeaker. (Dearborn City Council via YouTube Screenshot)

Dearborn city council president Mike Sareini told Fox News Digital that the pastor’s claims are false.

"The City of Dearborn is an American city governed by the U.S. Constitution, the laws of the State of Michigan, and the City of Dearborn Charter," Sareini said. "Those laws apply equally to every resident, regardless of religion or background. Everyone is treated the same."

"There is no evidence of preferential treatment for any religious group. These accusations are unfounded, and I challenge anyone to present evidence otherwise," Sareini continued.

"Dearborn is home to approximately 30 churches and 10 mosques," he added. "Most recently, pastors from throughout Dearborn spoke at a press conference and publicly confirmed that people of different faiths live together peacefully in Dearborn, without the conflict being alleged."

Fox News Digital reached out to Dearborn mayor Abdullah Hammoud and the Dearborn Police Department for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

articles.title: France, Saudi Arabia agree on $7bn theme park project near Paris
articles.excerpt:
Saudi Arabia and France boost cooperation: agreements reached on theme parks, AI and defence

France and Saudi Arabia have announced plans for a six-billion-euro ($7bn) amusement park near Paris, foll...
articles.body_text:
Saudi Arabia and France boost cooperation: agreements reached on theme parks, AI and defence

France and Saudi Arabia have announced plans for a six-billion-euro ($7bn) amusement park near Paris, following talks between French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman at the Elysee Palace.

The agreement was among a raft of deals signed on Monday as Macron and Prince Mohammed, who is also known as MBS, seek to boost economic and defence ties between their two countries.

Macron’s office said the amusement park project will see the construction of three theme parks, one of which is expected to be manga-themed, near Cergy-Pontoise, about 30km northwest of Paris. The project is expected to create roughly 22,000 jobs and will be led by Qiddiya, an investment arm of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund.

Macron called the project “extraordinary” and said it would create a “new global destination” on the scale of Disneyland Paris. He thanked Qiddiya and Saudi Arabia for their “trust” in French talent, framing the investment as a win for his “Choose France” drive to attract job-creating foreign capital.

“We’re not done surprising the world. Very proud of this achievement,” he added.

The project stemmed from a discussion between Macron and MBS in December 2024 in Riyadh, where they discovered their “shared passion” for manga, “and in particular Dragon Ball Z”, an adviser to the French president told reporters.

The other agreements, signed in a ceremony attended by Macron and MBS, span energy, artificial intelligence, aviation financing, transport and health.

Al Jazeera’s Bernard Smith, reporting from Paris, said there was also “a letter of intent signed, reinforcing cooperation on defence – an exchange of expertise on cybersecurity, AI training and military training”.

“The Saudi Arabian defence market is a significant market for French defence manufacturers, as Saudi Arabia looks for new strategic partners,” he said. “The French government wants to make sure it still has a hand in, is still working with Saudi Arabia on the country’s defence.”

The French presidency said two other contracts were signed with French companies during the Saudi crown prince’s visit: one for the marine logistics company CMA CGM to help develop Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah Islamic Port on the Red Sea, for $434m; and the other with rail transport group Alstom to supply metro carriages for Riyadh’s metro, for $580m.

The visit marks MBS’s third official trip to France and comes as Saudi Arabia pursues security ties beyond its traditional partnerships. It was also the Saudi crown prince’s first trip abroad since signing the trilateral Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkiye and Pakistan earlier this month.

Beyond the economic and defence agenda, Macron and MBS also issued a joint statement addressing several regional flashpoints.

The two sides called for a negotiated end to the conflict between the United States and Iran and demanded a return to normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

They also welcomed the US-brokered agreement on Hamas’s disarmament while pressing for a sustainable ceasefire in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. They affirmed support for Palestinian statehood and called for Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory.

They went on to condemn attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia as well as on commercial shipping. The two men also voiced support for Syria’s stability and recovery.

articles.title: ‘Like smoking a cigarette’: Indonesia chokes on haze as blazes intensify amid super ‘El Niño’
articles.excerpt:
In Indonesia’s Kalimantan, fires have ravaged tens of thousands of acres, with suffocating smoke reaching Malaysia and putting Singapore on alert

Suwadi can barely see five metres in front of him whe...
articles.body_text:
In Indonesia’s Kalimantan, fires have ravaged tens of thousands of acres, with suffocating smoke reaching Malaysia and putting Singapore on alert

Suwadi can barely see five metres in front of him when he steps outside his home in Indonesian Borneo.

Each breath, he says, feels “like smoking a cigarette”.

It has been like this for weeks in Kalimantan, the Indonesian side of Borneo island, where fires have raged across tens of thousands of acres of land, including ancient rainforest, triggering a trans-boundary haze now threatening Malaysia and Singapore.

In West Kalimantan there has been a spike in emergency room visits, with about 5,000 people arriving with respiratory symptoms each week since July, compared with 500 per week in the first half of the year, health ministry data shows.

Children continue to go to school and adults to work, but many are suffering from the unhealthy effects of breathing in thick smoke, constantly. “What about babies, the elderly, and pregnant women who are exposed to this?” asks Suwadi.

Some classes have been suspended, with parents urging schools to switch to online learning.

Fires each year in Kalimantan are often blamed on “slash and burn” techniques used to clear land for plantations that produce palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.

Authorities say this year’s “super” El Niño may be intensifying the blazes, with the weather phenomenon expected to peak in September.

Experts have warned the worst could be yet to come as the dry season continues into October, and the rains that could extinguish the fires look unlikely before November.

The haze is fast becoming a regional issue, with Malaysia and Brunei agreeing to raise it at Asean as thick smoke from forest and peatland fires drifts across the border.

On Tuesday, the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, was the most polluted city on earth, followed by Jakarta, according to air quality monitoring company IQAir. Almost 600 schools in the Malaysian state of Sarawak on Borneo island closed due to hot and dry conditions. Singapore went on alert.

On social media, Indonesians have tried to draw attention to the issue – highlighting the huge blazes in Kalimantan, and also in Sumatra, West Papua, and in Lombok where a fire destroyed a traditional Sade village over the weekend.

Forestry ministry data shows that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) have burned nationwide this July alone.

On Monday, the Indonesian president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered authorities to revoke the business permits of corporations suspected of directing the land clearing, state news agency Antara reported. Indonesian police arrested 72 people suspected of starting fires in Borneo and Sumatra, with most accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations.

The response comes as regional experts fear this could be another devastating fire year, with many of Indonesia’s most severe blazes occurring during El Niño cycles. In 2015, another El Niño year, more than 6m acres were burned, with trans-boundary haze again plaguing neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.

During a recent visit to the region, Prabowo promised government resources to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps.

But some Indonesians have expressed frustration at what they see as government inaction against the companies allegedly involved.

Indonesia’s unique rainforests are home to peatland ecosystems, which should be naturally resilient to fire when water tables remain high.

However, drainage networks built to clear land for pulp and oil palm plantations have robbed the soil of its natural capacity to retain water, experts say.

Fires on degraded peatlands are more difficult to control because they burn deep underground, says Justin Sentian, a professor in climate change at Universiti Malaysia Sabahand. And they produce thick, acrid smoke.

“If authorities only act after hotspots appear, they will forever be playing catch-up,” says Sentian. “True prevention must address the soil itself by halting the conversion of peatlands and actively restoring degraded areas.”

On Monday another fire broke out near the factory where Suwadi works in Kalimantan. With houses burning and smoke everywhere, Suwadi says he is afraid for the future of the region.

“The fire is getting dangerously close to homes,” he says, “People are [in] panic now.”

With Agence France-Presse and Associated Press

articles.title: Sydney shark attack survivor describes moment she came to face-to-face with ‘monster’
articles.excerpt:
In her first media interview since the June incident, Leah Stewart, 34, says her thoughts while being bitten were of her one-year-old daughter

An Australian woman who lost an arm after a shark attack...
articles.body_text:
In her first media interview since the June incident, Leah Stewart, 34, says her thoughts while being bitten were of her one-year-old daughter

An Australian woman who lost an arm after a shark attack at a beach in Sydney’s eastern suburbs has recalled the moment she came face-to-face with the “monster”.

Leah Stewart, a 34-year-old teacher and mother of a one-year-old daughter, was attacked by a large shark while on a morning swim at Coogee beach on 13 June.

She remained in a critical condition for more than two weeks while receiving treatment for life-threatening injuries that required the amputation of her arm.

In a snippet from her first media interview since the attack, Stewart recalled that her first thoughts during the attack were of her daughter.

“It was holding onto my leg, then I just thought of August. I thought, ‘She’s not going to have a mum. She’s going to grow up without a mum,’” she told Nine Entertainment.

“I couldn’t handle that. I didn’t want her to not have a mum.”

Through tears, Stewart said the shark’s “face was horrific” and that she would “never forget its face … it was a monster.”

In an update to a fundraiser set up to cover Stewart’s medical procedures and support her family, she said on Sunday that she had been “focused on my healing” and thanked donors.

“After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I’m so happy that I’ve progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this,” she wrote.

“I’ve been actively trying to do everything in my power to get back to some sort of normal life. I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and me from all over the world.”

The GoFundMe page has raised more than $558,925 since the June attack. Donations have now been turned off.

“I want to say the biggest thank you for looking after me, for caring for my family, and for being generous enough to help my family through this,” Stewart wrote.

“What you’ve offered has given us enough to recover, to stay in our home, and to give us options for further medical treatment down the road.”

Stewart ended the note by saying she felt as though she had been “given a second chance at life”.

“I’m not going to waste it. As I get better, I know I’ll make something of this second chance and aim to give back even more in generosity, care and love.”

articles.title: Freddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ to go on display at V&A
articles.excerpt:
Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee

Eight famous costumes worn by Freddie Mercury, including the outfit featured on the cove...
articles.body_text:
Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee

Eight famous costumes worn by Freddie Mercury, including the outfit featured on the cover of Queen’s debut album and the catsuit from the video for Bohemian Rhapsody, are to go on display at the V&A in London this autumn to mark what would have been the singer’s 80th birthday.

Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things, a free trail developed with Mercury’s former fiancee and close friend Mary Austin, will run from 24 October 2026 to 17 January 2027. Austin is lending seven of the looks, which span Mercury’s career from the 1970s to his final years.

Among them is a monochrome ensemble worn for an early Queen gig at Imperial College and pictured on the cover of the band’s eponymous debut album. Also on display will be the “Mercury Wing” catsuit, designed by Wendy de Smet and worn during the A Night at the Opera tour in 1975-76, as well as in the groundbreaking Bohemian Rhapsody video.

Mercury’s crown and cloak, designed by Diana Moseley and worn during Queen’s 1986 Magic Tour, will also feature. He wore the outfit for the band’s final live performance at Knebworth that year. The display will also include a costume from the Made in Heaven music video, as well as accessories and items from his personal wardrobe.

The trail takes its name from a remark Mercury made in 1978: “I like to be surrounded by splendid things. I want to lead a Victorian life surrounded by exquisite clutter.”

Austin first met Mercury when she was 19 and he was 24, while they were both working around Kensington’s Biba fashion scene. Mercury, born as Farrokh Bulsara on 5 September 1946 in Zanzibar, was selling his artwork and vintage clothes from a stall in Kensington Market. They became engaged on Christmas Day 1973, the year Queen released their debut album.

Their relationship ended in the mid-1970s, but they remained close for the rest of Mercury’s life. When he died in 1991, he left Austin his Kensington home, Garden Lodge, and his possessions.

Austin has described Mercury’s clothes as central to the image he created as a performer. “The clothes were part of that exploration,” she said in A Life in Lyrics, due to be published in September. “Freddie understood early on that he wasn’t just wearing clothes; he was providing an image to match the scale of the space and the vastness of the crowd.”

Austin said the clothes and costumes to be displayed at the V&A “tell a hugely important part” of Mercury’s story both on and off the stage: “Never mere accoutrements, his costumes and clothes were essential to his performances, creative vision, and wider self-expression, carefully designed to create a lasting visual and emotional impact that has reached across the generations and still reverberates today.”

The installations have been designed by Tom Piper, whose work includes productions for the Royal Shakespeare Company, the Tower of London poppies and the V&A’s Alice: Curiouser and Curiouser and Taylor Swift | Songbook Trail.

Each of the trail’s six stops will be staged differently, using sets, sound and lighting to evoke moments from Mercury’s career.

Kate Bailey, the V&A’s senior curator of theatre and performance, said the display would explore Mercury’s “love of ‘splendid things’” and his interest in art, design and fashion.

articles.title: Europe’s heatwaves threaten insurers’ earnings, rating agency S&P says
articles.excerpt:
Rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people, could drive up premiums

Europe’s intense heatwaves could hit insurers’ earnings as companies face a rise in cl...
articles.body_text:
Rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people, could drive up premiums

Europe’s intense heatwaves could hit insurers’ earnings as companies face a rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and worsening health conditions, the rating agency S&P has said.

While a long summer of extreme heat will have increased drought and wildfire-related claims, the rating agency said there would also be fallout for life and health insurers, and for the reinsurers who provide financial protection to insurance companies.

That could ultimately translate to higher premiums for customers, as insurers try to cover increased payouts to policyholders.

Europe’s heatwaves, paired with its ageing population, have created a perfect storm, with the health impacts of high temperatures falling disproportionately on older people. That fact has resulted in a wave of life insurance claims over heat-related deaths, and increased demand for private medical services, at a time when rising temperatures have not yet been fully reflected in original contracts.

Between 2004 and 2024, the share of people aged 65 and over in the EU rose from 16.4% to 21.6%, while the proportion of those aged 80 and over rose from 3.8% to 6.1%. “The increasing share of elderly people – who are particularly vulnerable to heat stress – suggests that heat-related mortality in Europe is likely to rise,” the S&P report said .

About 9,000 of the 10,650 excess deaths recorded during the 22-28 June heatwave were among those 65 and over, as rising heat exacerbated underlying conditions such as heart disease and dehydration.

“Beyond heat-related deaths, it’s also deteriorating health conditions and the resulting increase in treatment and hospitalisations that might weigh on re/insurers’ financials and, subsequently, increase premiums,” the report said.

A study in The Lancet Planetary Health recently found that people aged 60 and over face dangers from exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought. Older adults sweat less, their hearts work harder in the heat, and their blood vessels are less able to widen, limiting their capacity to stay cool.

In the UK alone, the four-day heatwave in May and eight-day heatwave in June together caused 2,877 excess deaths, compared with the 1,504 seen during the summer of 2025.

There has been little reprieve, with the mercury rising beyond 40 degrees Celsius across Europe earlier this month, breaking records in countries including Slovakia, Austria and Hungary earlier this month. And given heatwaves can affect large regions and last for weeks, they could end up compounding financial risks for insurers.

While the heat had not yet hurt company ratings – which indicate how safe or risky their shares or bonds are for investors – that could change over the medium term to long term “as extreme summer temperatures become more frequent and intense, and Europe’s population continues to age”, S&P said.

“We will continue to monitor their impact on the performance of rated re/insurers,” it added.

articles.title: NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer
articles.excerpt:
NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening

Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments wil...
articles.body_text:
NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening

Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS.

The move comes amid concerns that only two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointments when asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date.

The rollout is being described as a “gamechanger”, offering a “discreet and convenient option” to encourage more women to get screened.

The kits contain a swab to collect a sample from the vagina. This is then posted back to the NHS free, where it is tested in labs for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV).

If high-risk HPV is detected, patients will then be asked to attend a cervical screening appointment with a clinician.

HPV is a group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. About 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers.

Starting on Tuesday, eligible women between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations via the NHS app, text message, email or letter.

They will then be able to order a kit through the app or website. The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040.

Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS.

“Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.”

Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected.

The latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. It means about 4 million women are not up to date, according to NHS estimates.

“There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,” said Mann.

“So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.”

Athena Lamnisos, chief executive of the Eve Appeal, welcomed the move, saying that self-testing at home would be a “step-change” for many women.

Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “Cervical screening is a powerful tool that saves lives – it can prevent cervical cancer or spot it at an earlier stage when treatment is more likely to be successful.

“While it’s best for cervical screening to be done by a nurse or doctor, there are barriers that make it challenging for some people to attend. At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them.”

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the aim was to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. She said: “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.”

articles.title: At least 35,000 excess deaths recorded in Europe’s back-to-back heatwaves
articles.excerpt:
True figure likely to be much higher as it only covers about half of continent and does not include August totals

At least 35,000 more people died during Europe’s four record-breaking, back-to-back h...
articles.body_text:
True figure likely to be much higher as it only covers about half of continent and does not include August totals

At least 35,000 more people died during Europe’s four record-breaking, back-to-back heatwaves this summer than would normally be expected, according to incomplete figures from barely half the continent.

Excess mortality in three of the EU’s larger countries – Germany, France and Spain – alone has already exceeded 25,000, according to the provisional national figures, and experts say the toll will rise significantly once August totals are consolidated.

The consecutive heatwaves across western Europe since May shattered all-time historical temperature records across hundreds of weather stations, and France recorded its hottest national average day on record.

Records fell for three straight days in Germany in late June, when 46 stations topped 40C (104F), while Spain endured persistent highs above 42C. Scientists say human-made global heating is making such extreme events more frequent and intense.

The death toll is highest in Germany, which late last week reported an estimated 14,000 heat-related deaths from 6 April to 9 August. The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) public health agency said 9,600 people had died in the week of 22-28 June alone.

Systematically compiled EU-wide excess mortality figures, available since 2008, show the only other summer week in which a higher rate of additional deaths has been recorded was in July 2022, when Covid-19 was still active.

This summer has been by far the worst for heat-related deaths in Germany since records began. The previous high in the EU’s most populous country was 8,900 in 2018. Heat-related deaths during normal summers are often below 2,000, RKI said.

Figures from the Carlos III health institute’s mortality monitoring system suggest 4,947 deaths in Spain can be attributed to heat between May and this week, making 2026 Spain’s worst year on record for heat-related deaths, exceeding the 4,520 recorded in 2022.

Different countries calculate and present their data in different ways. Spain and Germany model estimated heat-related deaths in real time, comparing daily temperatures and mortality rates to calculate deaths attributable to heat.

Such estimations are necessary because heat is rarely stated as a direct cause of death. In most cases, heat aggravates a pre-existing health conditions such as respiratory or cardiovascular disease, and victims die of a heart attack, stroke or kidney failure.

Final attribution can take weeks or even months, and many countries have yet to release figures even for early August. Karl Lauterbach, a former German health minister, said last week that figures released so far would probably prove to be underestimates.

France, where more than 500 weather stations recorded temperatures higher than 40C and at one stage 98% of the country was under heat alerts, reports an initial “all causes” excess death figure and definitive attribution later.

Its national health agency said last week that “all cause” excess deaths between late May and 22 July stood at 7,300. August figures were not yet available and initial data was based on electronic death certificates, which account for only 80% of total mortality, it said.

Italy, whose national heat surveillance system uses local municipal data, meaning it is often subject to significant delays, has so far only reported incomplete real-time indicators rather than a consolidated national death toll.

Modelling suggests 2,700 more people died than usual between 22 and 28 June alone and epidemiologists have said the country’s total heat-attributable death toll would probably be between 5,000 and 8,000 by the time it is formally recorded.

Other European countries to have already reported excess death tolls include the UK, where the health security agency said in July that its modelling suggested the May and June heatwaves had resulted in 2,877 heat-associated fatalities in England.

Belgium has said its preliminary data shows it recorded a 39% increase in mortality between 18 and 29 June, equating to 1,222 additional deaths, and the Netherlands has said at least 900 more people than usual died between 22 June and 5 July.

A rapid modelling study cited by the European Commission estimates that 1,070 more people than usual died in Poland during the late-June heatwave, and Swiss public health authority data suggests excess heat-related deaths of 220 in the same week.

Early figures from Luxembourg, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Denmark indicate about 40 excess deaths in each of those countries. Agence France-Presse has calculated that areas inhabited by more than 80 million Europeans experienced temperatures above 40C this summer.

The World Health Organization said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had increased by more than 30% over the past 20 years and was on course to climb significantly as a result of the climate crisis and population ageing.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Postpartum is real, but child killing demands accountability, veteran prosecutor says
articles.excerpt: Jonathan Hatami, who rose to national prominence after prosecuting the murder of Gabriel Fernandez by his mother and her boyfriend in Los Angeles, says anyone who hurts a child, whatever the reason, s...
articles.body_text:
Jonathan Hatami, who rose to national prominence after prosecuting the murder of Gabriel Fernandez by his mother and her boyfriend in Los Angeles, says anyone who hurts a child, whatever the reason, should not be considered a victim themself.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

While failures by people, medical professionals and systems around Lindsay Clancy deserve scrutiny, nothing should erase a parent’s responsibility for killing a child, according to a veteran prosecutor who said he's concerned that public support for the Massachusetts mom is overshadowing the killing of her three young children.

Clancy is accused of killing her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

But as the case has drawn national attention, Clancy has also attracted supporters both online and in-person at the courthouse, and experts have warned that that support has taken attention away from the victims.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S THREE CHILD VICTIMS FORGOTTEN AMID CROWDS OF SUPPORT: MOTHER OF SIX

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"Nobody who murders children is a victim no matter what they’re suffering through," said Jonathan Hatami, a veteran child abuse prosecutor. "You're never a victim if you murder people because victims don't do something. Something happens to them."

(L) Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in this undated photo. (R) Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony from her former mother-in-law at her murder trial in Plymouth Mass., Tuesday Aug. 18, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/ Facebook and Jonathan Wiggs/Pool The Boston Globe via AP)

The defense does not dispute that Clancy caused the deaths — but she has pleaded not guilty and is contesting criminal responsibility.

Hatami has spearheaded a number of high-profile cases against child abusers in Los Angeles, California, including the murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, who was tortured and killed by his mother and her boyfriend. Gabriel's killing exposed a series of missed red flags by the county's Department of Children and Family Services and inspired a Netflix docuseries.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE SCORES ‘EXTREMELY HELPFUL’ PSYCHOSIS CONCESSION AS EXPERT FLAGS NEXT HURDLE

Exterior view of the home of Patrick and Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, MA on Wednesday, Feb. 15, 2023. Lindsay Clancy allegedly killed their three children here before attempting to take her own life on Jan. 24, 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

"Gabriel Fernandez was tortured and murdered by his mom and her boyfriend — however, there were a lot of other people...that were responsible," Hatami told Fox News Digital. "There were a lot of people that missed signs through the eight or nine months of Gabriel's torture. There were a lot of people in government, in law enforcement, social workers, who missed all these different signs that really could have saved Gabriel — and they didn't do it. However, Pearl Fernandez and Isauro Aguirre were ultimately responsible for the torture and murder of Gabriel and were prosecuted for that and they were convicted of that."

LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

Lindsay Clancy reacts as doctors testify about efforts to save her children Friday, July 31, 2026. Prosecutors allege that after she strangled them with workout bands, she jumped out of a second-story window, causing injuries that left her paralyzed. (Josh Reynolds for Daily Mail /Pool)

In Clancy’s case, he argued, many of the people and systems around her deserve scrutiny — but that should not turn her into the central victim of the story. In his view, she's been too much of the focus.

"Instead of about the three victims who were innocent kids," he said.

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

While failures of government and the child welfare system were investigated after Gabriel's murder, that didn't take responsibility away from the killers, he said. And in the Clancy case, he said he sees a risk that the focus on her mental health could eclipse the three children who were killed in their own home.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I didn't see people out in the streets cheering on Pearl Fernandez because there were other people that were somewhat responsible for what happened to Gabriel," he said. "And the same thing plays in this case. Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death. She admitted to strangling them to death with exercise cords."

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Clancy's defense has said she sought help repeatedly as she struggled with depression, sleeplessness, suicidal thoughts and voices urging her to harm herself and the children.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

"If you murder your children, you need to be held accountable and responsible for that," Hatami said. "No matter what the whys are, no matter what reasons are."

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

SUSAN SMITH ELIGIBLE FOR PAROLE AGAIN AFTER BEING DENIED RELEASE FOR DROWNING HER 2 SONS IN 1994

If convicted of any of the three counts of first-degree murder she faces, Clancy would see a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Your children should be your life. And if you take their life, you should, as a person, want to be punished for that," Hatami said.

Fox News' Sarah Rumpf-Whitten and Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

articles.title: NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of Chinese follower
articles.excerpt:
New Zealand police released a picture of Shulai Wang

A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family....
articles.body_text:
New Zealand police released a picture of Shulai Wang

A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family.

Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu.

Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music.

During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023.

She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark",  along with several other female followers.

Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master".

Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables.

The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined.

In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard.

The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage".

The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice.

Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year.

On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand.

Shulai Wang's body was found near the marina at Gulf Harbour in Auckland

New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China.

In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded.

Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents.

Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music.

During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends".

During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang.

"Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

articles.title: Massachusetts woman suspected of killing police officer husband found dead
articles.excerpt:
Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home

A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Mond...
articles.body_text:
Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home

A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Monday, six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said.

Karen Solomon, an advocate who called for improvements and greater awareness of police mental health issues, had disappeared after Worcester police officer Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home just before 5.30am on 18 August. Officials had named Karen Solomon a suspect and said she was believed to be armed.

“We believe this case is a tragic murder-suicide that occurred,” the Worcester police chief, Paul Saucier, said at a news conference Monday.

Two people who worked at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding human remains nearby, and officers recovered a woman’s corpse, Saucier said. A final ID was still pending, but authorities said they were confident it was Karen Solomon.

A handgun found near her body was not a Worcester police service weapon, and investigators were working to determine who owned it.

On 19 August, authorities released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops, just minutes after officers responded to the couple’s home and found her husband’s body.

Kurt Solomon, who had served 31 years with the police department, was mortally injured with a sharp object, authorities have said.

Worcester county district attorney Joseph Early Jr said Karen Solomon had been at the house on the morning of her husband’s death, and investigators were looking to question her. An arrest warrant issued over the weekend charged her with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

Police handed out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area. An intensive law enforcement search that included local, state and federal agencies centered on the area near the couple’s Worcester home and a reservoir about a mile (1.6km) away. Authorities had deployed drones, boats and tracking dogs.

Karen Solomon, 58, co-founded the group First Help, which advocates for the mental health of police officers. She also wrote two books – Hearts Beneath the Badge and The Price They Pay – about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders.

In a 2020 interview on the Dr Phil show with Phil McGraw, she said police departments often offered little help to the families of officers who took their own lives.

In a statement read by Saucier during Monday’s news conference, the Solomon family thanked law enforcement for helping them find some answers.

“The nightmare of the past week has left our family heartbroken and rudderless,” the family said. “The compassion, dedication and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.”

A wake for Kurt Solomon was scheduled for Tuesday, and his funeral for Wednesday, the police chief said. The local police union president, Thomas Duffy, described him as “a tremendous human being” who was like family.
