articles.title: Caste divides make scorching summers harder in a parched corner of India
articles.excerpt:
Mamta, from the Dalit (formerly untouchable) community, says access to water in her village becomes harder in the summers

A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first...
articles.body_text:
Mamta, from the Dalit (formerly untouchable) community, says access to water in her village becomes harder in the summers

A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first of as many as 10 journeys she would make that day.

Carrying three empty plastic buckets, she walked a few hundred metres to the nearest handpump in her village in Jalaun district, in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of northern India. Temperatures in parts of the region were soaring above 40C.

The taps installed under a government drinking water scheme had been dry for two years, she said, leaving most of the village's 1,000 residents dependent on a handful of handpumps.

Mamta said collecting enough water for her 11-member family and their livestock took hours. But the heat was not her only obstacle.

Mamta belongs to the Valmiki community, part of the Dalits - groups once regarded as "untouchable" under India's centuries-old caste hierarchy and which continue to face widespread discrimination.

She said she waited until members of the village's dominant castes finished using the handpump before approaching it.

"If they are standing there, we cannot fill water. We have to wait until they leave," she said.

Afterwards, she said, some upper-caste residents poured water over the pump to "cleanse" it.

Bundelkhand, a semi-arid region that spans several districts in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, is notoriously drought-prone. It faced several major droughts between 2002 and 2016, making it almost a symbol for water scarcity in a country where several regions face similar hardships.

The rocky terrain of the Bundelkhand plateau means it can store little groundwater. Erratic rainfall and hotter temperatures have also made access to water unpredictable despite several government and community-led conservation efforts.

A study of more than a century of weather records found temperatures had risen across almost the entire region, and in recent summers, parts of Bundelkhand have neared 48C.

Bundelkhand is a dusty and rocky region where temperatures often climb above 40 degrees

Residents and researchers say worsening heat and water stress are putting new pressure on an old divide.

As more families compete for scarce shared water, Dalits who have long faced barriers in accessing it are encountering those inequalities more often.

"Conflict over water is not new," said Mitashi Singh of the Centre for Science and Environment.

"What is changing is the role hotter summers are playing in making water scarcer and intensifying tensions that already existed."

Local officials reject claims that the region faces water shortages or caste discrimination at public water sources.

Dominant-caste residents interviewed by the BBC also denied discriminating against others, although they acknowledged growing pressure on water supplies.

Ram Gopal Singh, who is in his 50s, pointed to several abandoned village wells.

"These wells have been dry for almost 20 years," he said. Other sources had dried up or become polluted, while unreliable tap connections had pushed more families towards handpumps.

Everyone tried to collect water in the cooler morning hours, he said, leading to arguments over turns and how much each family could take.

"But there is no caste-based dispute at these handpumps," he insisted.

There are just a handful of handpumps in Mamta's village

Dalit residents interviewed by the BBC described something different.

There is no formal queue at the pumps, they said. Instead, families try to collect water at different times to avoid confrontations.

Mamta said she usually went very early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

"The fear of being targeted stays with me throughout," she said.

About 50km away in Shahjahanpur, Shiv described a similar experience.

He said members of his community would not approach the handpump while dominant-caste families were using it.

"No matter how hot it is, even if we have to wait for hours for one bucket of drinking water, we wait because we do not have a choice," he said.

In summer, when his family needed more water, those waiting periods became more frequent.

"Even if my parents are thirsty, we sometimes wait for hours before we can drink."

Mamta says she either goes early in the morning or late in the afternoon to fill her buckets

Three years ago, Shiv's mother Parmi Devi said she was assaulted after an argument with a member of a dominant caste at a village handpump.

"I was thrashed and beaten up and thrown on the ground three times," she alleged.

"It was not just about water. It was because of our caste."

Devi filed a police complaint alleging assault. No arrests have been made yet.

Such disputes have surfaced repeatedly in complaints documented by the Dalit Dignity and Justice Centre (DDJC), a non-profit organisation in Uttar Pradesh.

The group said police registered 113 cases under India's law against caste-based atrocities in the area in 2025.

Kuldeep Singh Baudh of DDJC told BBC Hindi a majority of the complaints it tracked during the hottest months of May and June involved water, though the organisation has not published a detailed breakdown.

"To truly understand [the heat's] impact, you have to see it from the perspective of the communities that are the most excluded," he said.

The office of District Magistrate Rajesh Kumar Pandey rejected the allegations.

"There is not even one instance wherein caste-based discrimination is being practised when it comes to access to water in the region," it said in a statement.

Shiv's mother Parmi Devi was allegedly assaulted for using a handpump

The statement also disputed claims of water shortages, pointing to the federal government's Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to provide piped drinking water to every rural household, and other local efforts to restore ponds and recharge groundwater.

There have also been wider efforts to tackle Bundelkhand's water crisis. Traditional water bodies, including ponds and check dams, have been revived across the region, while women-led groups known as Jal Sahelis work in villages to monitor supplies and promote water conservation.

Mukul Sharma, a researcher on caste and environmental politics, said increasing water supplies was only part of the solution.

Climate change is "not the origin of these injustices, but a threat multiplier", he added.

More water alone will not solve the problem if caste still shapes who gets to use it, Sharma said.

That morning in May, Mamta waited beside the handpump as other families filled their buckets, three empty plastic containers at her feet.

In cooler months, she said, she made the journey only a few times a day. In summer, it could be eight or 10, each trip determined partly by who was already at the pump.

When her turn came, she filled her buckets and carried them home. Later that day, she would return.

articles.title: Woolworths’ Ooshies craze causes Coles sales slump with parents shopping at rival supermarket to collect toys
articles.excerpt:
Coles full-year results show that despite gaining market share over past 12 months, sales fell over four weeks of ‘competitor’s collectables campaign’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest u...
articles.body_text:
Coles full-year results show that despite gaining market share over past 12 months, sales fell over four weeks of ‘competitor’s collectables campaign’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Woolworths’ latest Disney “Ooshie” collectables have not only captivated Australian children, they have led to a short-term slump in competitor Coles’ sales.

The latest rubber figurine promotion was scheduled to end on Tuesday, but strong customer interest meant Woolworths prematurely ran out of Ooshies a week ago.

Coles on Tuesday released its full-year results, showing it had grown supermarket sales and gained market share against Woolworths in the 12 months to June.

Growth continued into July but then slumped amid a “competitor’s collectables campaign”, Coles announced.

That was a reference to Woolworths’ recent Ooshies promotion of Disney, Marvel and Star Wars characters that could be collected after a customer spent $30.

The Coles chief executive, Leah Weckert, said the moderation in sales was a “temporary impact” lasting nearly four weeks. It mostly affected bricks-and-mortar shops rather than online shopping.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Michael Toner said the impact of the Woolworths campaign could scare Coles investors.

Ooshies, designed to fit onto the top of pens or pencils, come in generic packaging. It’s not clear what figure you’ve recieved until the pack is ripped open, mostly by keen children who then trade the Ooshies at home or school in an attempt to collect all 40 characters.

Schoolchildren also stage Ooshie battles where they flick the characters to try and knock down competitors’ figures.

Woolworths has hosted dedicated swap meets across the country in recent weeks to help customers complete their collections.

Adult customers have turned to online marketplaces to trade Ooshies. A dedicated Facebook Ooshie swap group added almost 2,500 members in the past week and now has more than 45,000 members.

The 2019 Ooshies craze culminated in two farmers destroying a rare lion Ooshie live on TV in a protest against online bullying.

Prof Gary Mortimer, a consumer behaviour expert at the Queensland University of Tehcnology, said Ooshies could help children build social skills – similar to when youngsters traded marbles last century.

“Those games taught us the art of competing, fair-play, learning to deal with disappointment and celebrating wins,” Mortimer wrote on LinkedIn.

“Swaps taught us ‘friendly’ negotiation skills, compromise and the principles of value exchanges.”
 But some schools have moved to shut down trading.

A Queensland independent school, Bellevue Park state school, posted on Facebook that it had banned Ooshies due to “distractions, conflict and unfair trading”.

“We need your support to make sure these items remain safe at home and are not bought to school where they can become lost, damaged or stolen,” it wrote in a Facebook post.

One Sydney after-school care centre said it was no longer allowing the toys because there had been “disputes around trading and ownership, and situations where children have become upset or distressed”.

The bans are a badge of honour for Alan Ngov, the chief commercial officer at Headstart International, the company that developed Ooshies.

“You know it was a good one when you get banned from the school yard! What an amazing campaign from the Woolworths, Disney and Headstart teams!” he wrote on LinkedIn.

Nearly two-thirds of parents surveyed by polling company YouGov said they changed their shopping behaviour due to the Ooshies promotion, including shopping at Woolworths more often.

One in five adult Ooshies collectors planned to sell the products online, YouGov’s survey released this week found. Millennials were most keen on collecting them, while baby Boomers were interested in passing them on to loved ones.

Fumin Rianto, a research director at YouGov Australia, said the products had struck a chord and developed a genuine online resale economy.

But “there’s a real conversation to be had about where all these tiny plastic collectables end up once the craze fades,” Rianto said.

Environmental groups are concerned about the volume of plastic that will eventually end up in landfill.

Kirsten Junor, the chief executive of not-for-profit Reverse Garbage, said the carbon emissions used to make and transport Ooshies outweighed any benefit.

“It’s just future landfill,” she said in a video posted on social media earlier this month.

“Kids don’t need them. We don’t need them. The planet doesn’t need them. Stop making them. You don’t need to get a reward every time you go shopping for what you need.”

Woolworths has said the Ooshie figures are made from “97% recycled thermoplastic rubber”. The company has offered dedicated collection bins in some stores to recycle the figures.

Weckert, the Coles boss, said on Tuesday the supermarket planned to continue its own promotional collectable campaigns in the future.

Coles reported its net profit rose 1% to $1.09bn in the year to June. Its supermarkets increased their profit margin on earnings from 5.3% to 5.7%.

articles.title: Woodside scraps long-term emissions and clean energy targets despite windfall oil profits caused by Iran war
articles.excerpt:
Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn in the six-month reporting period

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking n...
articles.body_text:
Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn in the six-month reporting period

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Woodside Energy has scrapped its long-term emissions and clean energy targets, even after enjoying a period of windfall oil profits caused by the Iran conflict.

Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn ($A2.33bn) in the six-month reporting period, according to financials lodged on Tuesday, after the price of crude surged amid disruptions to global supplies.

It expects more trading gains by redirecting barrels to markets paying premium prices for barrels of oil.

At the same time, the Perth-headquartered company said it would drop its commitment to invest $US5bn ($A7bn) in new energy products, such as hydrogen, by 2030.

It has placed its new ammonia business in the US under strategic review; an asset previously described as one of Woodside’s highest potential options for decarbonising power sources.

Under the new chief executive, Liz Westcott, Woodside is doubling down on fossil fuels while shifting the company further away from clean energy and decarbonisation targets.

Westcott told analysts on Tuesday the company would “retire” its so-called scope 3 investment and abatement targets, which refer to emissions produced by its customers, because the targets “were established in a different market context”.

“The reality is that markets for emerging lower carbon opportunities, including hydrogen, ammonia, and carbon capture and storage, have developed more slowly than anticipated,” Westcott said.

The company said that its new energy business would be guided by “customer demand and commercial markets”.

Woodside is one of a growing list of large oil companies amassing profits because of the Iran conflict at the same time as emissions-fuelled climate change affects communities around the world.

A recent run of deadly heatwaves in the northern hemisphere, made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels, has reignited calls for those same fossil fuel companies to shoulder the growing environmental costs of rising temperatures.

Brett Morgan, investor campaigns manager at climate activists Market Forces, said big polluters must be held accountable for environmental damage.

“Woodside has ditched its already feeble scope 3 emissions reduction and new energy investment targets, despite years of investor pressure demanding stronger climate action,” Morgan said.

He said major Woodside investors, including Australian super funds, must respond by demanding an end to the company’s plan to expand fossil fuel operations.

Woodside declared an interim dividend of US57c per share, up from US53c last year.

articles.title: Scots College students charged with sexual assault of teen girl appear in court
articles.excerpt:
Three boys, two aged 14 and one aged 13, on bail and yet to enter a plea after alleged assault in Sydney’s east

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, fr...
articles.body_text:
Three boys, two aged 14 and one aged 13, on bail and yet to enter a plea after alleged assault in Sydney’s east

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Three teenage boys from a prestigious Sydney private school who allegedly raped a 14-year-old girl in an alleyway in Sydney’s eastern suburbs have faced court for the first time.

On Tuesday the three boys, two aged 14 and one 13, all pupils at Sydney’s Scots College, had their matter heard in Surry Hills children’s court but remained outside the courtroom.

The court heard the trio, who are on bail, had been issued an AVO which states that they cannot go within 200 metres of the girl they allegedly assaulted.

The boys, who cannot be named for legal reasons, were charged after an alleged incident on Wednesday, 22 July.

One of the 14-year-olds and the 13-year-old are charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others and two counts of aggravated sexual touching.

The other 14-year-old was charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others and one count of aggravated sexual touching.

Court documents which provide brief detail of the allegations against them allege that the incident occurred over 55 minutes.

Judge Sue Duncombe also warned media in court about the need to protect the identities of the teenagers after the court heard some of their names had been revealed in online comment sections.

“This matter has obviously attracted a lot of media attention so far,” Duncombe said. “There have already been some repercussions on some of the young people from being identified.”

The matter was adjourned for eight weeks until 20 October.

On Monday, defamation lawyer Rebekah Giles, who is representing two of the boys, sent a letter to media outlets reminding them of their obligations under the Children Criminal Proceedings Act, which prohibits the identification of any children involved in criminal proceedings.

The accused trio are on bail and are yet to enter a plea.

The Scots College, where the trio are students, is one of Sydney’s oldest and most expensive boys’ schools, charging fees of up to $47,000 a year.

The school has said it is cooperating with police regarding the alleged rape.

“Scots College is aware three students are under investigation by NSW Police in relation to an alleged incident that occurred outside school hours,” the school said in a statement on 13 August.

articles.title: Israel’s Netanyahu claims Iran tried to kill one of his sons
articles.excerpt:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that Iran tried to kill one of his sons, but gave no details on when or where the alleged plot took place or which of his sons was targeted.

Neta...
articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that Iran tried to kill one of his sons, but gave no details on when or where the alleged plot took place or which of his sons was targeted.

Netanyahu’s allegation on Monday came as his coalition trailed in opinion polls ahead of the general election in October, in the wake of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

The war began with a joint US-Israeli strike on Tehran that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and four members of his family, including his daughter, Boshra, and his 14-month-old granddaughter, Zahra.

According to The Jerusalem Post, Netanyahu made the claim about the alleged Iranian plot against his son during a phone interview with Channel 14, a conservative Israeli outlet known for favourable coverage of the government.

“This is an unbelievable case. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to murder him, tried to murder one of my sons,” Netanyahu said.

He was responding to reports that one of Israel’s security agencies had declined to provide a security detail for Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is running neck and neck with Netanyahu for the next prime minister ahead of elections.

Netanyahu voiced support for around-the-clock protection for Eisenkot, saying it was “not a luxury”.

“Without that, [the Iranians] will succeed,” he said.

Netanyahu has two sons and a daughter. Both of his sons and his wife were granted extended personal protection by Israeli authorities in July, according to The Jerusalem Post.

His elder son, Yair, 35, has spent extended periods in the US city of Miami since early 2024, drawing controversy in Israel over the cost to taxpayers of protecting him.

Iran, meanwhile, has promised revenge for the killings of Khamenei and his family.

Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, was named the new supreme leader a week after Ali Khamenei’s death.

Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since his appointment, but in a message published on the occasion of funeral ceremonies for his father, he pledged to “avenge the blood” of the former supreme leader.

articles.title: Amnesty says India used lethal weapons on ‘Cockroach’ protesters

Amnesty says India used lethal weapons on ‘Cockroach’ protesters

articles.title: Syria off US terror blacklist after nearly 50 years as Trump admin clears investment hurdle
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The United States on Monday formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a move Secretary of S...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The United States on Monday formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a move Secretary of State Marco Rubio said eliminates the final major barriers to investment and economic recovery in the country.

Rubio said in a statement that he had authorized the formal rescission after a mandatory 45-day congressional notification period ended.

President Donald Trump had initiated the countdown in July after confirming to Congress that Syria’s government had ceased supporting acts of international terrorism.

"I have also delisted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham’s (HTS) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT)," Rubio said Monday.

FORMER ASSAD-ERA PRISON CHIEF CONVICTED OF TORTURE IN US FEDERAL COURT, MARKING A HISTORIC FIRST

Syria’s president secured a major diplomatic boost as the U.S. removed the country from its terrorism blacklist, clearing key barriers to investment. (BING GUAN/POOL/AFP via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The actions, he said, represent "another historic step by President Trump to give the Syrian people a path to prosperity."

Rubio said Washington had taken unprecedented steps over the past year to provide sanctions relief to the Syrian people.

He pointed to Trump’s June 2025 executive order, "Providing for the Revocation of Syria Sanctions," which accelerated sanctions relief by terminating the Syria Sanctions Program and the national emergency with respect to Syria while directing reviews of other Syria-related sanctions and terrorist designations.

"These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," Rubio said of the Syrian government.

Al-Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 in an offensive led by HTS rebels. Syria had been on the State Sponsors of Terrorism list since 1979, with the designation in force throughout al-Assad’s rule.

BRIEF ALCOHOL BAN IN DAMASCUS SPARKS CONCERNS ABOUT PRESIDENT AL-SHARAA'S VISION FOR SYRIA

Secretary of State Marco Rubio shakes hands with then Syrian interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa at the Lotte New York Palace Hotel, on the sidelines of the 80th United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations headquarters, Monday, Sept. 22, 2025. (Bing Guan/Pool Photo via AP)

"In the past year, the Government of Syria has taken significant steps to counterterrorism, to include formally joining the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS in November and conducting operations to disrupt the terror networks of ISIS, al-Qa’ida, Hizballah, and Iran-aligned groups," Rubio said.

He added that rescinding Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism and HTS’ designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist "eliminates the final major barriers for private-sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy."

EVANGELICAL LEADER SAYS US MUST PROTECT SYRIAN CHRISTIANS FROM ATTACKS BY JIHADI TERRORISTS

Syrians gather in Umayyad Square, waving the Syrian revolution flags as they continue their celebrations after the overthrow of the 61-year Baathist regime and the end of the Assad family era in Damascus, Syria on Dec. 27, 2024. (Emin Sansar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Aug. 22 that lifting the designation would help restore Syria’s links to the global financial system and encourage investment following nearly 14 years of war.

"There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.

"Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said in a statement, adding that it is "in line with President Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria."

The governor of the Central Bank of Syria said Monday that lifting Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism is a "historic step that returns it to its natural place within the global economic system."

On Monday, Trump also posted a photo on Truth Social of al-Sharaa and al-Shibani holding his signed June 2025 executive order directing sanctions relief for Syria.

Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Colombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdown
articles.excerpt:
Far-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermath

Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espri...
articles.body_text:
Far-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermath

Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes.

In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes.

De la Espriella said the first joint operations involving the police and the migration authority should begin “this very week”.

“Let the coordinated operations begin to track down illegal immigrants: first, those committing crimes; second, those who have not regularised their status and who will have to be deported immediately,” de la Espriella said during a cabinet meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the Caribbean city that has in effect been turned into an alternative capital.

He echoed the “Americans first” rhetoric of his ally, US president Donald Trump, saying that from now on it would be “Colombians first, Colombians second and Colombians third”.

The Colombian president has joined other Trump-aligned leaders in the region who have also tightened migration rules, including Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast.

De la Espriella’s order is facing criticism from the opposition and human rights activists, who say it will end a migration policy that endured for more than a decade under both rightwing and leftwing governments and benefited above all migrants fleeing the humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Venezuela.

Although he used the anti-immigration rhetoric characteristic of other far-right candidates during his campaign, his platform focused chiefly on his promise to pursue an iron-fist policy against criminal groups.

In the same announcement, he also declared that all gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining, extortion and smuggling were “terrorists and we will treat them as such. Whatever happens, we will defeat them, by reason or by force.”

The president did not directly mention Venezuelans when discussing immigration, but they account for roughly 90% of all migrants in the country. Of the 2.8 million Venezuelans living in Colombia, about 848,000 are in an irregular situation, including 193,000 children and adolescents.

The leftwing senator María José Pizarro Rodríguez reposted the president’s announcement and asked whether he was “proposing a Colombian ICE against fellow Latin Americans”, in reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She added that the “order to deport irregular migrants is pure xenophobia and aporophobia”.

“Instead of persecuting people fleeing poverty and violence, regularise their status. There are thousands of migrants who work hard and contribute to the economies of the countries that receive them,” she wrote.

The Colombian newspaper El Tiempo reported that sources within the migration department believe the agency does not have enough staff to carry out the operations De la Espriella has promised.

Analysts have also noted that under Colombian law there is no such category as an “illegal” immigrant, as De la Espriella said, but rather migrants in an “irregular” situation, since being in the country without the proper documentation is not a crime.

articles.title: DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
articles.excerpt: Kinshasa, DR Congo – President Felix Tshisekedi is due to leave office in 2028 under the current Constitution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Yet with more than two years to go, a battle over...
articles.body_text:
Kinshasa, DR Congo – President Felix Tshisekedi is due to leave office in 2028 under the current Constitution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Yet with more than two years to go, a battle over the rules governing what happens when his mandate ends is already reshaping Congolese politics.

In May, Tshisekedi said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue. The remarks revived opposition fears that constitutional reform could eventually open a path beyond the existing two-term limit.

Under the current constitution, the president is elected for five years, renewable once, while the number and length of presidential terms are protected from constitutional revision.

Tshisekedi’s camp says the country needs institutional reform. Opponents of the reform fear the process could ultimately be used to change the rules governing presidential succession.

The dispute is unfolding as the DRC fights a rebellion in the east led by M23, an armed group that operates within the broader Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition that controls Goma and Bukavu, the capitals of North Kivu and South Kivu.

With an opposition mobilisation planned for September and Tshisekedi preparing to outline an inclusive national dialogue, the confrontation is entering a critical phase.

The confrontation accelerated in June when the Parliament of the Democratic Republic of the Congo passed legislation setting out conditions for organising a referendum.

The Constitutional Court ruled in July that the law complied with the constitution, while raising concerns about some of its provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi formally asked the presidents of the National Assembly and Senate to reconsider the legislation in light of the court’s observations. The National Assembly said the fresh deliberation would be placed on the agenda for its September session.

The legislation provides for a constituent assembly followed by a referendum in the event of what it describes as a “major dysfunction” of state institutions.

Critics of the process say the mechanism could eventually be used to alter provisions that currently prevent Tshisekedi from seeking a third term. The government, meanwhile, has presented constitutional reform as a broader institutional issue rather than an explicit bid to extend the president’s tenure.

The main opposition group campaigning against the process is known as C64, or the Article 64 coalition. Its name refers to Article 64 of the DRC’s constitution, which calls on citizens to oppose anyone who takes power in violation of the constitutional order.

C64 says it will resist any attempt to use constitutional reform to extend Tshisekedi’s mandate beyond 2028. The coalition announced a nationwide mobilisation for September 15, with demonstrations in Kinshasa expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple, the seat of parliament.

The dispute has already spilled onto the streets.

Thousands demonstrated in Goma and Bukavu on July 28 against proposed constitutional changes and any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s time in office.

In Kinshasa, protesters are expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple.

For C64, the destination is deliberate: the coalition wants to take its protest to the institution at the centre of the constitutional process.

Jean-Marc Kabund, a Congolese opposition politician, told Al Jazeera that no constitutional revision, referendum or legal manoeuvre should be allowed to circumvent the current constitution.

He warned that this happening while the country is at war could deepen divisions and threaten national cohesion.

The constitutional dispute is unfolding alongside a conflict that has transformed eastern Congo.

M23 and the AFC have seized large areas of territory, including Goma and Bukavu. The Congolese government accuses Rwanda of supporting M23, a charge that Kigali denies.

The war is also raising questions about the 2028 elections.

Tshisekedi has warned that elections may not be possible if the fighting continues, arguing that it would be difficult to organise a credible vote while parts of the country remain outside government control.

Emmanuel Bugama, a Congolese political analyst based in Bunia, told Al Jazeera that national interests should come before political disputes.

“The nation’s best interests should take precedence over these political squabbles,” he said.

In Goma, the argument is being watched from a city no longer under Kinshasa’s control.

Gentil Mulume, a civil society activist in Goma, told Al Jazeera that any constitutional change extending Tshisekedi’s mandate would not be recognised in territory controlled by M23 and the AFC.

“If Tshisekedi dares to amend this constitution to extend his term of office, it will not be recognised here,” he said.

Mulume said the dispute was part of a deeper divide between Kinshasa and the east. He argued that continued Tshisekedi rule could be viewed there as a form of domination and that self-determination should be part of the political debate.

His comments illustrate how a constitutional confrontation in Kinshasa is being interpreted in territory already beyond the government’s effective control.

There is also a more basic question: how much do ordinary citizens understand about the proposed changes?

Kevin Kalala, a 30-year-old mobile-credit retailer in Kinshasa, told Al Jazeera that he does not know enough about the constitution to take a position.

“We do not know what our constitution entails,” he said. “The Congolese state should start by teaching us about our constitution.”

Kalala said citizens should first be shown which provisions need changing, why they need changing, and what the benefits would be.

“I am neither for nor against amending the constitution,” he said.

As tensions rise, Tshisekedi has proposed an inclusive national dialogue involving political parties, civil society and religious groups.

While in Libreville, Gabon, on August 16, he said he would soon address the nation to set out his vision and the contours of the talks. The date and format of the dialogue have yet to be announced.

Tshisekedi has ruled out sitting with people he accuses of siding with Rwanda or the armed rebellion.

Martin Fayulu, who challenged Tshisekedi in the 2018 presidential election, has called for former President Joseph Kabila and Corneille Nangaa, the political leader of the AFC, to participate.

For now, the constitutional dispute is running alongside the war in the east and the uncertainty over the 2028 elections.

The question is no longer only whether the constitution will change. It is whether Congo’s political forces can agree on the rules for what happens when Tshisekedi’s current mandate ends.

“We are certainly heading towards one of the most decisive periods in our recent history,” Bugama told Al Jazeera. “The country is under the control of an armed group, whilst the government in Kinshasa is posturing over constitutional reform instead of tackling what matters most.”

articles.title: Search continues in Tunisia as migrant boat sinking sparks protests
articles.excerpt:
Tunisia protesters march after deadly migrant boat sinks

Volunteers in Tunisia have continued the search for two people still missing after a boat carrying 15 migrants sank off the country’s southeas...
articles.body_text:
Tunisia protesters march after deadly migrant boat sinks

Volunteers in Tunisia have continued the search for two people still missing after a boat carrying 15 migrants sank off the country’s southeastern coast, as the city of Ben Guerdane reeled from violent protests sparked by the tragedy.

Footage, verified by Al Jazeera, showed volunteers in the city of Zarzis heading out to sea on fishing boats on Monday to search for the missing.

The migrant boat, believed to be headed towards Italy, sank late on Friday after setting off from a location between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane with 15 mostly young people on board. It sank about 14 nautical miles (26km) off the coast of Zarzis.

Only one person survived, having drifted at sea for about 48 hours before being rescued by a commercial vessel, according to Tunisian media.

The bodies of 12 people were recovered by Sunday, the Tunisian National Guard said.

The deaths have sparked a wave of grief and anger, triggering violent protests in Ben Guerdane on Sunday night. According to the Tunisian National Guard, some 14 people on the boat were from Ben Guerdane, and one was from Zarzis.

The protesters burned tyres and blocked roads, while police responded by firing tear gas to disperse the crowds. The protesters demanded better living conditions and economic development, saying a lack of opportunities and years of marginalisation are pushing young people to undertake dangerous sea crossings to Europe in search of a better life.

Mostafa Abdelkebir, the head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights, said those on board included seven members of the same family. He told the Reuters news agency on Monday that a hospital in Ben Guerdane has received at least 19 bodies of migrants recovered from the sea over the past two days.

It was not clear if all the bodies were from the boat that sank. Abdelkebir told Reuters that genetic testing was being carried out to identify the bodies and determine how many had been on board the boat.

Some in Tunisia have called for a national day of mourning over the deaths.

Imad Oulad Jibril, a lawmaker, on Sunday called it “the tragedy of a nation that sees its youth fleeing the hardships of the land only to be swallowed by the sea”.

The opposition Democratic Bloc party tied the sinking to Tunisia’s economic strains, saying: “When crossing the sea becomes easier than living in Tunisia, we must ask: Who is at fault?”

Tunisia has seen similar tragedies in recent years, including the Kerkennah disaster, in which more than 100 people died or went missing in 2018 after the sinking of a migrant boat. The incident led to the dismissal of the then-interior minister. In Zarzis in 2022, at least 18 people died after another migrant boat sank, sparking weeks of protests.

Tunisia’s southeastern coast lies just 145 km (90 miles) from the Italian island of Lampedusa.

The central Mediterranean is considered the deadliest migration route in the world, according to the International Organization for Migration, which says at least 821 migrants have died or gone missing on the route this year – more than double the toll over the same period last year.

Across the Mediterranean as a whole, at least 1,065 people have died or gone missing, according to the group.

articles.title: Trump admin eyes historic mass visa revocation targeting up to 200K asylum seekers: report
articles.excerpt:
‘Border czar’ Tom Homan evaluates the State Department’s crackdown on visas after it revoked more than 175,000 from foreign criminals and fraud suspects on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

The Trump administrat...
articles.body_text:
‘Border czar’ Tom Homan evaluates the State Department’s crackdown on visas after it revoked more than 175,000 from foreign criminals and fraud suspects on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

The Trump administration is reportedly preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum in the U.S.

The State Department is expected to announce the sweeping action in the coming weeks, The Associated Press reported, citing internal documents and two U.S. officials.

The effort would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to foreigners who later sought asylum. If carried out, the move would mark the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history and could face legal challenges, according to the outlet.

FOREIGN DRUNK DRIVERS COULD FACE SWIFT BOOT OUT OF COUNTRY UNDER TRUMP'S 'AMERICA FIRST' CRACKDOWN

The State Department is reportedly expected to announce the sweeping action in the coming weeks. (Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images)

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

Pigott did not confirm how many people could be affected, saying the revocations would occur on a "rolling basis" and the total remained "dynamic," according to the AP.

The move would not automatically lead to immediate deportations.

Foreigners with pending asylum cases would generally be reclassified but would lose their status as business or tourist travelers, officials told the AP.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks Aug. 6 during a roundtable at the State Department in Washington, D.C. If carried out, the move would reportedly mark the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said Monday that asylum should not be used to bypass immigration laws.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau wrote on X. "Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

TRUMP TELLS FOREIGN STUDENTS: OVERSTAY YOUR VISA, FACE THE CONSEQUENCES

Christopher Landau speaks during a panel discussion in February at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Orlando, Fla. Landau said Monday that asylum should not be used to bypass immigration laws. (Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

B1 visas are typically issued for business travel, while B2 visas cover tourism, family visits and medical care. Currently, applicants must demonstrate that they plan to return to their home countries.

The potential revocations come as the Trump administration cracks down on what it considers abuse of the immigration system. The State Department has revoked roughly 175,000 visas over the past 18 months, according to The Associated Press.

The State Department could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

articles.title: US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism
articles.excerpt:
US President Donald Trump welcomed his Syrian counterpart Ahmed al-Sharaa to the White House last year

The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting wh...
articles.body_text:
US President Donald Trump welcomed his Syrian counterpart Ahmed al-Sharaa to the White House last year

The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy.

US Secretary Of State Marco Rubio said the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism.

The Trump administration has embraced Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head as the leader of an al-Qaeda off-shoot.

His Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations.

HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016.

In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew former president Bashar al-Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration.

The US hopes to bring Syria into its orbit rather than that of Russia or China. But the risks remain significant, with Syria still far from secure and lacking representative government. It is also at the centre of growing tensions between its neighbours Israel and Turkey.

Rubio said Monday's move, which had been initially flagged in July, would give the Syrian "a path to prosperity".

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability."

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani greeted the news as a "historic step", according to state-run news agency SANA.

"We will continue working to remove the effects of isolation and create an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect," he said.

Last year, the US also revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists.

Syria's removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism - where it had been since 1979 - leaves just three remaining: Cuba, North Korea and Iran.

The listing carries financial sanctions, restrictions on US foreign aid and defence exports and sales and can also penalise people and other countries that trade with the sanctioned state.

A destructive tornado has torn through villages in southern France, injuring more than 40 people.

An eyewitness from the village of Verzeille recorded the tornado forming beneath a thunderstorm. Winds of more than 100km/h (62mph) ripped the roofs off homes in Pomas.

Local authorities say about 2,800 households were still without electricity on Monday evening, while several roads were blocked.

articles.title: Ex-NBA player tells Laura Ingraham why WNBA can't ban him: 'I identify as a woman'
articles.excerpt:
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom discusses his confrontation with Chicago Sky player Natasha Cloud, after which he was removed from a game against the Indiana Fever, on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

For...
articles.body_text:
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom discusses his confrontation with Chicago Sky player Natasha Cloud, after which he was removed from a game against the Indiana Fever, on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom joined Laura Ingraham on "The Ingraham Angle" Monday night to set the record straight following his chaotic courtside ejection from Sunday's Indiana Fever-Chicago Sky matchup.

Freedom was escorted out of Wintrust Arena late in the third quarter after Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud unleashed an explicit, profanity-laced tirade against him after simply celebrating a 3-pointer by Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Turkish-American former basketball player and human rights activist Enes Kanter Freedom is seen prior to a game between the Indiana Fever and the Chicago Sky at Wintrust Arena in Chicago, Ill., on Aug. 23, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Freedom, who sat baseline wearing a shirt defining "woman" as an "adult human female," explained to Ingraham that he attended purely out of love for basketball and to back Cunningham, an athlete who has faced relentless backlash for defending female sports.

ENES KANTER FREEDOM MET WITH HOSTILE WNBA FANS EN ROUTE TO FEVER-SKY MATCHUP

But after Freedom put his hands up following a made bucket, Cloud immediately confronted him with personal insults, mocking and screaming that Cunningham was "not going to sleep" with him.

"I actually loved the game and enjoyed the game," Freedom told Ingraham.

Former basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom and Natasha Cloud #9 of the Chicago Sky yell at one another during the second half between the Chicago Sky and the Indiana Fever at Wintrust Arena on August 23, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) (Michael Reaves/Getty Images)

Former basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom looks on courtside during the first half between the Chicago Sky and the Indiana Fever at Wintrust Arena in Chicago on Aug. 23, 2026. (Getty Images)

"This is my passion... first half I watched the game; it was an amazing time. They put Sophie Cunningham in. I remember around the last three-minute mark she shot the ball and I put my hand in the air to celebrate it. Then Natasha Cloud saw that. Literally the next possession, (Cloud) came back and yelled at me, '(Sophie Cunningham) is not going to sleep with you.'"

Freedom admitted the outburst left him stunned.

PAYTON MCNABB: THE BACKLASH AGAINST SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM PROVES THE GOALPOSTS HAVE MOVED

"I'm just confused at that point," Freedom said. "I'm here to protect women and support Sophie Cunningham."

Cloud escalated the confrontation with a slew of F-bombs in front of a section filled with young children, Kanter noted.

"The next possession, (Cloud) started to yell and cuss at me," Freedom said.

"I was like, there are so many kids in those stands. There are so many teenagers... a lot of F-bombs. She started to come toward me and I literally got up... I'm like, what did I do? She should be the one to be thrown out of the game."

SKY COACH PRAISES NATASHA CLOUD AFTER HEATED VERBAL ALTERCATION WITH ENES KANTER FREEDOM

Instead of penalizing Cloud for charging at Enes and dropping vulgarities, arena security escorted Freedom out of the building.

Sophie Cunningham #8 and head coach Stephanie White are shown during a game against the Toronto Tempo at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on June 16, 2026. (Getty Images)

Enes’ shirt has apparently become kryptonite for a WNBA still unable to answer the most basic question in women’s sports.

"I'm shocked it's a controversial topic nowadays, but it is," Freedom noted.

After Enes' appearance on Sunday, the league sneakily drew a line in the sand, telling media outlets like Front Office Sports that Kanter Freedom will not be eligible to get drafted into the WNBA.

He reminded them of their loose standard of what a woman is.

"I am a woman. I should be allowed to play," Kanter told Ingraham. "Article 13 Section 1 says if you identify as a woman, then you are allowed to play. I identify as a woman, so yes I can play."

"They're terrified because I might actually get drafted next year."

Enes' primetime appearance comes as former NBA pick Royce White warned the WNBA will likely attempt to ban Freedom from future games to protect themselves on a PR level and dodge further scrutiny over its gender policies.

While Fever head coach Stephanie White tried to play media gatekeeper postgame by labeling the chaos a mere "social media thing," Freedom's interview proves the opposite.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: John Harbaugh calls it 'reasonable to assume' Malik Nabers will be available for Giants in Week 1 vs Cowboys
articles.excerpt: Colin Cowherd and John Middlekauff unveil their five bold NFL predictions, including Justin Herbert winning 2+ playoff games, the Denver Broncos missing the playoffs, Maxx Crosby getting traded to the...
articles.body_text:
Colin Cowherd and John Middlekauff unveil their five bold NFL predictions, including Justin Herbert winning 2+ playoff games, the Denver Broncos missing the playoffs, Maxx Crosby getting traded to the Chicago Bears and more.

Malik Nabers has shocked many New York Giants fans in training camp with just how great he looks on the gridiron with his teammates after an offseason shrouded in mystery and doubt about whether he’d be ready for Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys on "Sunday Night Football."

Now, after practicing without a red non-contact jersey Monday, head coach John Harbaugh gave yet another encouraging update on the Giants 2024 first-round pick that points in the right direction for his availability to start the season.

Harbaugh told reporters Monday that it is "reasonable to assume" Nabers is trending toward being available right out the gate for the Giants, which is an incredible sign for the wide receiver who tore his right ACL and had meniscus damage in Week 4 last season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers stands on the field before the game against the Minnesota Vikings at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., on Aug. 15, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES)

"Probably moving the best we’ve seen him look," Harbaugh said about Nabers, as he wore a regular white jersey alongside his fellow receivers during 11-on-11 and 7-on-7 reps on Monday.

In fact, Harbaugh believes that "very reasonable" contact with defenders during practice is something he’d be fine seeing Nabers go through.

ODELL BECKHAM TOLD GIANTS COACH HE'S READY TO 'GO OUT ON MY SWORD' TO EARN ROSTER SPOT

"Those are all kind of things that you can assume," Harbaugh said when asked about Nabers in terms of Week 1 availability. "It’s just based on watching the guy practice. The only thing I know more than you guys know is what the docs and the trainers tell me, as far as his rehab. And that’s doing well. He’s doing really well with that. He’s strong. He’s in a good place."

It wasn’t a fully padded practice for the Giants, but Nabers has been spotted wearing the red non-contact uniform for quite a bit now.

Seeing Nabers not wearing the non-contact jersey, though, is exactly what Harbaugh had planned for the team’s top pass-catching option. He noted not wanting to see Nabers go from no contact to 100% to start the season.

And for Nabers himself, he said last week "my soul has been dead for so long," hinting at how badly he’s wanted to get back on the field and do what he loves. He also noted the "dog" in him is starting to wake up, and he’s only been trending in an upward trajectory since that first training camp practice surprised fans with just how well he was moving in and out of his routes.

New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers (1) looks on before the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at MetLife Stadium on Sept 21, 2025. (Vincent Carchietta/Imagn Images)

Now, it shouldn’t be expected that Nabers gets time in the Giants’ final preseason game against the New York Jets this week. The teams won’t be holding any joint practices either, so Nabers’ journey to Week 1 availability will have to continue against his teammates.

But the build is there, and the LSU product continues to check boxes in his new head coach’s head.

"I thought he looked good. Look at the tape later, but he was moving well. …It was a good practice for him today," Harbaugh said.

Nabers and quarterback Jaxson Dart have developed quite the chemistry already, but the Giants’ 2025 draft choice out of Ole Miss only had one quarter with Nabers during his first career start before the devastating knee injury.

Wide receiver Malik Nabers speaks to the media during New York Giants Rookie Minicamp at Quest Diagnostics Training Center on May 10, 2024 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Sarah Stier/Getty Images)

Giants fans are itching to see what Dart, who had 24 total touchdowns in 14 games last season, and Nabers, who had 1,204 yards in 15 games his rookie year in 2024, can do across a full 17-game slate.

The Giants will take on the Cowboys at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 13 in a primetime matchup at 8:20 p.m. ET.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Utah teen charged with killing mother, 8-year-old brother as mystery of final hours unravels: police
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 17-year-old Utah boy is accused of killing his mother and 8-year-old half-brother after prosecutors say a masked fig...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 17-year-old Utah boy is accused of killing his mother and 8-year-old half-brother after prosecutors say a masked figure matching his build was caught on camera roaming the neighborhood in the hours after a late-night shooting.

Saratoga Springs police arrested the teen on Aug. 14 after a 17-month investigation involving dozens of search warrants, hundreds of pieces of evidence and extensive forensic testing, the department said.

The teen was booked into juvenile detention after detectives screened two counts of first-degree murder with the Utah County Attorney’s Office, police said.

Prosecutors later charged him in juvenile court with two counts of aggravated murder and obstruction of justice, according to charging documents obtained by KSL.

16-YEAR-OLD NC GIRL CHARGED IN TRIPLE MURDER OF FAMILY MEMBERS, ARRESTED IN TENNESSEE WITH 28-YEAR-OLD MAN

Jessica Orton Lyman and her son, Eli Painter, are pictured in a family photo. (Alex Orton Facebook)

The state said it intends to seek to move the case to adult district court, the outlet reported. The teen’s identity has not been released because he is a juvenile.

PARENTS FOUND BURIED BEHIND HOME IN WEALTHY NEIGHBORHOOD AS POLICE LAUNCH INTERNATIONAL MANHUNT FOR SON

Police responded to a medical-assist call at the family’s home on Willowbrook Lane on March 28, 2025, and found Jessica Orton Lyman, 44, and Eli Painter, 8, suffering from gunshot wounds. Despite efforts to save them, both died, police said.

The victims’ remains were discovered after Lyman’s teenage daughter returned home the next morning, KSL reported.

A neighboring home-surveillance camera allegedly captured an argument around 11:30 p.m. the night before the victims were found, with voices investigators believe belonged to the teen and the victims.

Near midnight, a woman’s voice consistent with Lyman’s could be heard shouting, "What are you doing?!" Less than two minutes later, three gunshots were heard, one, followed by a brief pause, then two in rapid succession, according to the charging documents.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S FORMER DEFENSE EXPERT CALLS FOR DEATH PENALTY, SAYS INVESTIGATORS MISSED KEY EVIDENCE

Jessica Orton Lyman and her son, Eli Painter, are pictured with family members. (GoFundMe)

The teen later told investigators that he and his mother had argued that night, KSL reported.

Additional home-surveillance video allegedly showed a masked figure walking through the neighborhood between 2:34 a.m. and 2:59 a.m. on March 28.

Prosecutors said the person was consistent with the teen’s height and build, and that the mask and some clothing appeared consistent with items he had worn. The person’s route and gaps in the video suggested the weapon could have been discarded in several places, including the nearby Jordan River, according to the charging documents.

FBI and Saratoga Springs police dive teams later searched the river and surrounding banks for evidence. Police had previously said they had not recovered firearms in the investigation other than two BB guns found in the teen’s room, KSL reported.

The charging documents also allege investigators found gunshot residue on multiple clothing items, including clothes the teen wore the morning the victims were discovered. His DNA was allegedly found beneath one victim’s fingernails and on the waistband of shorts Lyman was wearing when she died, according to KSL.

DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

The Saratoga Springs Police Department investigated the 2025 shooting deaths of Jessica Orton Lyman, 44, and her 8-year-old son, Eli Painter. (Saratoga Springs Police Department)

A warrant unsealed last year detailed a search of the teen’s room, where detectives allegedly found handwritten notes mentioning "serology," "DNA" and "firearm testing." Another note read, "This is a murder story," KSL reported.

Police said the home was immediately secured as a crime scene and investigators began the extensive work of documenting the scene, collecting evidence, conducting interviews and pursuing leads.

Over the next 17 months, detectives executed dozens of search warrants, collected hundreds of items of evidence and reviewed extensive video, records and other information, police said.

Numerous pieces of evidence were submitted to forensic laboratories, and some examinations required significant time before investigators could take additional steps, according to the department.

"As additional evidence and forensic results became available, detectives continued to evaluate and corroborate the information developed throughout the investigation," Saratoga Springs Police Chief Andrew Burton said following the arrest.

COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID'

Jessica Orton Lyman and Eli Painter are pictured in an undated photo. (Alex Orton Facebook)

"Most recently, the examination of additional evidence, combined with the totality of the investigative work conducted over the past 17 months, placed our detectives in a position to identify a suspect and establish probable cause for an arrest."

The FBI, Utah State Crime Laboratory, West Jordan Police Department and Utah County Sheriff’s Office Evidence Team assisted in the case, police said.

The department said its work is not finished, and that investigators continue to conduct follow-up interviews and analyze additional information.

The arrest came after Lyman and Eli’s relatives spent more than a year publicly pleading for answers.

"Not a day has passed without feeling the weight of this loss. Our family is forever changed," the Orton family said in a March statement released as the one-year anniversary of the killings approached.

"We miss Jessica and Eli every moment — their laughter, their light, and the love they brought into our lives."

The family said at the time that it knew evidence was still being processed and urged anyone with information to come forward.

IDAHO MURDERS EVIDENCE LEAK TRIGGERS CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION FOR INSIDER WHO SPILLED SECRETS: REPORT

The FBI, Utah State Crime Laboratory, West Jordan Police Department and Utah County Sheriff’s Office Evidence Team assisted in the case, police said. (Al Drago for The Washington Post via Getty Images, File)

Following the arrest, the Orton family said it was grateful to the agencies that worked on the case but stressed that no prosecution could undo the loss.

"Today’s arrest marks an important step toward justice for our daughter and sister, Jessica Orton Lyman, and our grandson and nephew, Eli Painter," the family said in a statement released through police.

The family said it expects the person responsible to be held "fully accountable for their actions, without excuse, exception, or leniency."

Jason Painter, a family member of both victims, said Lyman was "a devoted mother whose strength and love touched everyone around her," while Eli was "a bright, loving little man whose laughter and curiosity brought joy to everyone who knew him."

"They were so much more than the tragedy that took them," Painter said. "Their lives were filled with love, and they deserved many more years together."

The families said they will continue to honor Jessica and Eli by remembering "the love they shared, the lives they lived, and the legacy they leave behind, not just how they were taken."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Utah County Attorney’s Office for additional comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump
articles.excerpt:
'Trump underestimates us': Doug Ford takes aim at US over tariffs

What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its goods to the US, actually have in this spiralling trade dispute with its sout...
articles.body_text:
'Trump underestimates us': Doug Ford takes aim at US over tariffs

What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its goods to the US, actually have in this spiralling trade dispute with its southern neighbour, who also happens to be the world's largest economy?

Canada is the top customer for 26 US states, including Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin. And it is in the top three for 45 of the 50 American states, suggesting Prime Minister Mark Carney has room to manoeuvre in a trade fight.

For now, Carney's planned Canadian retaliatory duties are strategic "dollar-for-dollar" countermeasures focused on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, electronics, pulp and paper - though the list is still being finalised.

Polls suggest a majority of Canadians would be unhappy if his government went in the other direction and made significant concessions to the US. That sentiment is shared by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of Trump's most vocal critics north of the border, who responded to the tariff threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass".

Canada's Finance Department said additional measures to protect workers and businesses would be announced on Tuesday.

Here are some areas where Canada can apply economic pressure.

Carney noted on Saturday that Canada supplies the vast majority of US natural gas and electricity imports and about 60% of crude oil imports.

"I don't think they want us to stop sending any of that energy," he said.

Squeezing the US on energy is not in the current countermeasures, although various political officials have said explicitly it wasn't ruled out - and not all provincial premiers have been keen to use that leverage.

Ford, whose Ontario province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry,  is open to how far the dispute could go and said that an "energy surcharge is on the table".

He briefly floated a 25% surcharge in 2025 on all electricity exports to the United States, which his government estimated would have impacted 1.5 million homes and businesses in Michigan, Minnesota and New York.

The country is also a major source of important commodities including potash - a product in fertiliser for which Canada is the world's top supplier.

"I'd love to see [Trump] run cars without any oil. I'll love to see him grow vegetables and fruit without the potash," Ford said on Monday. "President Trump underestimates us, and that's the biggest mistake."

Canada also has significant reserves of critical minerals like lithium, nickel and graphite.

The US is Canada's top destination for overall mineral exports, another point where Ottawa could apply pressure.

Ford here also took the lead, saying in an interview with the Associated Press that the US  "won't get a grain of sand out of Ontario".

Watch: "Absolutely ridiculous": Canadians react to new tariff tensions with the US

Canada has already proven that it can cause economic pain in the US.

Even before trade talks broke down, a decision by most provinces to ban US alcohol from liquor store shelves - in response to the first wave of US tariffs early last year - dealt a devastating blow to that industry in the US.

American wine had a significant collapse in exports, one the Wine Institute called the "most significant market disruption in decades".

US wine exports to Canada fell 78% year over year, a $357m (C$494m; £261m) loss in export value, according to government data. The distillers association reported similar numbers - saying provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70%.

That boycott remains in place in 11 of the 13 Canadian provinces and territories. The ban is a point of significant frustration for the Trump administration.

While that alcohol boycott has been put in place by political leaders, there are also grassroots decisions by many Canadians that have hurt their neighbour's economy - such as avoiding travel to the US.

Even with a slight uptick in road trips to the US in April, Canadians made 800,000 fewer trips that month compared to the same time in 2024, before Trump returned to office, according to national data.

The travel boycott has meant a loss of about C$3.3bn ($2.35bn; £1.75bn) in revenue for the US last year. Some American cities and states have appealed for Canadians to return through targeted advertisements and special deals.

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump threatens tariff hike on autos after Carney vows to retaliate

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal

Timing and Canadian political will could also be a tool for negotiations.

Canadians know they will feel economic pain in this dispute - financial analysists estimated the most recent tariffs of 50% on about $20bn of Canadian imports could trim between 0.3% to 0.6% off the country's GDP in the short term.

Still, a majority in the country broadly back Ottawa's decision to drive a hard bargain against the Trump administration, and other Canadian political leaders have shown a united front.

A weekend poll from Angus Reid indicated that some 76% of Canadians support Ottawa's decision to walk away from trade negotiations even as they worry for their own job security.

The US midterm elections are fast approaching, with the economy front and centre for voters and the Republican hold on Congress looking tenuous.

Two of the biggest Senate races are in Michigan and Maine, which both border Canada and send most of their exports there.

The Yale Budget Lab calculates that under current law, Trump's global tariffs will cost American households about $1,100 annually.

Any further increase in the costs of goods and the wider impact of the trade dispute on businesses could further sour the American public on the economy.

On Monday, Carney said that US workers will be hurt by Trump's most recent threat to increase tariff on autos and auto parts from Canada to 50% after 1 January.

"What is the message sent out to the workers in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Alabama? These workers depend absolutely on Canada, their largest consumer," he said, adding that Canada buys more American cars than the EU and other countries.

On CNN on Monday, British Columbia Premier David Eby noted US consumers will see the impact of the US tariffs in any number of goods.

"If you're building a new home, on plywood, if you're replacing your floor, on veneers, if you're getting married, on cut flowers, if you're going out fishing, on fishing poles," he said.

"It is a bizarre policy for Americans. It's going to hurt them."

Ford, one of the most vocal Canadian leaders opposing the Trump administration's tariffs, also did not rule out specifically targeting Republican US states with retaliatory measures and "making sure America's economy feels the pain".

As for the coming midterms, Ford said: "If I were allowed to, I'd be down there door-knocking".
